signalstubes:usageinfo-signalstubes-text:
Signals Tubes
Extends the Signals mod with program tubes. You imprint a finished network of Signals parts into a tube, and the tube then does the same work on the eight pins of one socket.

What the mod adds
• Program tube - carries a circuit. A blank one is made from a tube base, a tube core and a glass bulb.
• Tube socket - a block with eight pins; the tube sits in it and runs there.
• Circuit imprinter - reads the network connected to a socket and writes it into a tube. It has a plug on a cable and a probe.
• Tube copier - copies the program of one tube into a blank one, paid for with temporal gears.

What it is for
A network that fills a room fits into one socket. Put the tube into another socket and you have the same circuit twice, or use it as a part of a bigger network and imprint that again - this is how complex parts grow out of simple ones.
The machines of Signals Machines have a socket of their own: a tube in it controls the machine instead of wires, so a well-tuned control moves to every further copy of the machine as a single item.
A tube carries its author's name, and the author can lock it against copying and against looking at the circuit. Players who enjoy designing circuits can sell finished tubes to players who just want a working machine.
signalstubes:block-handbooktext-tubesock:
The socket holds one program tube and runs its program. It can be placed on floors, walls and ceilings.

An empty socket has eight pins, numbered 1-8, and wires connect to them like to any Signals part. With a tube in place only the pins the tube uses remain; the cap colour tells the role (green input, red output, dark setting), and aiming at a pin shows its name.

Seat a tube by right-clicking with the tube in hand; the socket turns as the preview shows - pins 1-3 towards the side you aim at. Take it out by right-clicking with an empty hand; the socket stays turned and its wires stay connected.
Put the same tube (or a copy of it) back by clicking the bed in the middle - it is seated as it was and the wires stay. A different tube rewires the socket: all its wires drop to the ground, and you connect them again to the new pins. A wrench turns the socket together with the tube; the wires move with the pins.

The imprinter's plug can be plugged into an empty socket: the network on its pins is then imprinted into a tube.
signalstubes:item-handbooktext-programtu:
A program tube carries a circuit imprinted in the imprinter. In a socket or in a machine's socket it behaves like the network it was made from.

A new tube is blank and has all eight pins without a meaning. Imprinting gives it a name, a description, up to eight named pins (input, output or setting), the author's name and a sign above the base that matches the circuit - the same circuit gives the same sign. The item's tooltip shows all of it.
The tube's colour is for you only: the base sets it, not the program. Use it to tell kinds of tubes apart.

Locks and authorship
The author is whoever imprinted the tube, and the tube carries that name for good. When imprinting, the author can set two locks. The copy lock stops anyone else from multiplying the tube: the copier refuses it for others, and whoever uses it inside a bigger network of their own loses it - it is soldered into the new tube, which inherits the lock. The view lock hides the circuit: others see only the name, the description and the pins, not how the circuit is wired inside. A locked tube of someone else cannot be overwritten or erased.
The locks protect the author's work, and that is what makes trading tubes possible: the author sells finished, working tubes, the buyer controls machines with them but can neither copy them nor look inside. A copy from the copier is the same as the original.
In the imprinter your own tube can be erased back to blank; tubes soldered inside come back then.
signalstubes:item-handbooktext-tubebase:
A ceramic base with eight pins, the foundation of a program tube.
Raw bases are formed from clay, four at a time, and fired like other pottery. In a pit kiln the base takes a colour from its clay; in a beehive kiln the layers give further shades. A cream base can be dyed in a barrel.
The colour passes on to the finished tube and has no effect on how it works.
With the Clay Casting mod the bases can also be cast: a plaster mold for two bases is filled with slip like the other molds of that mod.
signalstubes:item-handbooktext-tubecore: The inside of a program tube: metal parts, wire and crystal soldered together. The soldering iron wears while making it. The core, a base and a glass bulb make a blank tube.
signalstubes:block-handbooktext-imprinte:
The imprinter reads a network of Signals parts and writes it into a program tube.

How to
1. Put a tube into the socket on top (right mouse button) - a blank one, or an earlier tube of yours to overwrite.
2. Take the plug from its cradle (right-click with an empty hand) and right-click it into an empty socket or a machine's socket. That socket marks the border of the circuit: what is connected to its pins is imprinted, and the tube's pin numbers will be the socket's pin numbers. The cable reaches 24 blocks.
3. Mark the switches (knife switches) and delay blocks you want to control from outside with the probe - right-click them. They get a "setting" pin of their own: a signal on it turns the switch on; for a delay it sets the value (0 = the value from the time of imprinting).
4. Right-click the cabinet with an empty hand. In the window you name the tube, write a description, name the pins, tick the parts that go out to pins and the locks if you want them (see program tube), and press Imprint. What cannot be imprinted is highlighted red in the world, and the window names the reason.
Put the plug and the probe back by right-clicking their cradle, or the cabinet with the tool in hand; dropped tools come back by themselves.

What can be imprinted
Signals sources, resistors and connections, triodes and tetrodes, delays and switches. A switch toggled by an actuator is imprinted as a memory. Parts that read the world or the player (sensors, buttons, pressure plates, lamps) cannot be imprinted - they stay outside and connect to the pins. Devices of other mods may only sit directly on the socket's pins. Every wire must lead somewhere. If the circuit inside the tube is to react to something that cannot be imprinted, connect it to a socket pin and run a wire from that same pin into the circuit - the pin is imprinted as an input.

Tubes inside the network
Sockets with tubes inside the imprinted network are imprinted too. Your own or an unlocked tube is copied into the new one. A tube of someone else with any lock - and every tube that already holds soldered tubes - is soldered in: its program runs inside the new tube, but the tube itself is used up - it leaves its socket - and the new tube gets a copy lock. The window warns you before such an imprint (the warning can be switched off, and on again with the command /tubes warn on).
Erasing a tube gives the soldered pieces back. A new version of a circuit is imprinted into the same tube again; the author is whoever pressed Imprint.
signalstubes:item-handbooktext-imprinter: The plug on the imprinter's cable. Right-click it into an empty socket or a machine's socket; that decides which network is imprinted and how the pins are numbered. It belongs to its imprinter: it cannot be stored or given away, and it returns to its cradle when dropped or taken more than 24 blocks away. Pull it out by right-clicking the socket with an empty hand.

The imprinter's probe on a thin lead. A right-click marks a switch or a delay block in the network the plug is connected to; the marked part gets a "setting" pin when imprinted. Another click removes the mark. The same can be ticked in the imprinter's window. It belongs to its imprinter and returns when dropped.
signalstubes:block-handbooktext-tubecopi:
The copier writes the program of one tube into a blank one.

Put the tube with the program into the green socket and a blank tube into the red one (right mouse button; an empty hand takes them out again). Charge the copier with a temporal gear (right-click with the gear in hand; one gear 1000, at most 5000). A copy costs 10 plus the number of parts in the circuit and takes 5 seconds. The finished copy has the blank tube's colour and is otherwise the same as the original, including the author and the locks.

Control
Start the copy by right-clicking the cabinet with an empty hand, or with a signal on the Start pin. The State pin reports: 0 idle, 1 copying, 2 done, 10 nothing to copy in the green socket, 11 no blank tube in the red socket, 12 the tube cannot be copied, 13 out of charge. Any change in the sockets returns the state to 0.
A copy-locked tube is copied only by its author; a copier built by the author copies it on an automatic start too. A tube holding soldered-in tubes of others is never copied.

Automation
The sockets are open to the managed chutes and dampers of SignalsLink: the original can be swapped whenever the copier is not copying, the finished copy taken out when done. A run of copies is then a matter of the right wiring.
